Issued at 407 PM EDT Mon Jul 20 2026

Pattern / Forecast Synopsis: 

Northwest flow aloft remains in full swing as a robust shortwave 
passes through the Great Lakes region, with attendant occluding 
surface cyclone over northern Ontario. Associated occluded frontal 
boundary currently stretches from roughly the NW Lake Superior 
shore, passing NW of the Twin Cities (at the triple point) and a 
cold front runs toward Sioux Falls, SD... warm frontal boundary 
associated with the system running south from aforementioned triple 
point SSE through Saint Louis. Return flow will draw this front 
northward, but it is anticipated to stall out over western upper MI, 
south through WI and IL. Thus, most vigorous convection this evening 
to be suppressed SW of the CWA. That being said, good mid level 
support and diffluent 500mb and 300mb flow will still support deep 
convection over our neck of the woods, albeit, with a weakening 
trend, through later tonight. Following the passage of the occluded 
frontal boundary late tonight, lingering low level moisture should 
support additional diurnal convection through the day Tuesday and 
perhaps into Wednesday. Subtle ridging and subsidence should return 
by Thursday, aligned with surface high pressure passage, resulting 
in a drier day. Additional embedded 500mb height disturbances pass 
through over the weekend, perhaps supporting a returning rain / 
storm threat. 

Details: 

Severe Potential through Tonight: Current 1pm glance at radar and 
satellite shows the remains of some robust convection the initiated 
over western upper this morning making a run at eastern upper MI and 
the NW lower lakeshore. Anticipating this to continue weakening as 
it passes through the region, owing to a complete and utter lack of 
instability across the region... which may be an issue we fight 
through this event until better thermodynamics are forced into the 
region with the system's approach. As such, potential for a 
scattered shower or rumble of thunder anticipated to be confined to 
the aforementioned regions through the afternoon. Efficient
mixing has led to surface dewpoints across our area to dip into
the upper 50s and lower 60s... with the much more robust 
moisture holding over the western Corn Belt. This drier air will
likely make high instability difficult to attain, but won't 
completely zero us out. As such, with the approach of the 
frontal boundary later this evening, anticipate upstream 
convection, while weakening, to maintain itself into at least 
the western half of the CWA, partially aided by a plume of 
developing elevated instability courtesy of an accelerating low 
level jet upwards of 50kt. Anticipated convective evolution 
entails a transition from discrete supercells over western / 
central upper MI to a linear mode by the time it reaches our 
doorstep this evening. 

With the elevated nature of the storms, will see the threat of 
tornadoes diminish considerably, though SPC maintains a 2% risk over 
the region. The primary hazard will be damaging winds, which, 
despite the elevated instability profile, can still mix down with 
any gravity wave interactions to force those LLJ winds to the 
surface. As such, SPC has maintained the 15% risk for winds across 
the region. Severe hail, while possible (5% risk), is not 
anticipated to be overly widespread owing to the discrete mode not 
being able to be maintained. Current prognosis favors a window of 
roughly 7pm to 4am for the highest risk of severe weather across the 
region... and the general weakening trend is highlighted well with 
the SPC outlook... maintaining an Enhanced Risk (Level 3/5) over WI 
and western / central upper MI... a Slight Risk (2/5) eastward 
through most of our CWA, and a Marginal Risk (1/5) from the Lake 
Huron shores of Saginaw Bay north to the Alpena area. 

Hydro Concerns Tonight: Not to be lost in all the noise of the 
severe potential, torrential rainfall will be possible with these 
storms as they make it through the region. PWATS progged to go north 
of 1.25 this evening / tonight. Some CAMs do support localized 
training convection, which could easily put some embedded 2.00"+ 
rainfall amounts down over any area that realizes this. Overall 
current SPC HREF guidance shows two concentrated highest probability 
areas of convection across the Great Lakes: one just to our SW 
across WI and leaking into IL and IA... and another that 
originates from western / central upper MI and carrying through 
the Straits region and eastern upper (should be noted 
probabilities for thunder exist CWA-wide, these are just the 
highest probability regions across the Great Lakes / Midwest). 
Considering recent rainfall trends (including all the way back 
to April), the Tip of the Mitt region southeast to APN, along 
with portions of eastern upper, and the Leelanau / Antrim /
